name: Operating Systems & Systems Security
description: Kernel and OS-level security, isolation, sandboxing, virtualization, and access control.

uss.narrative:
The earliest cluster here (USENIX 2018) shows OS and systems security split between two fronts: hardening the kernel attack surface and reasoning about attacks after they happen. On the offensive/defensive boundary, "Meltdown: Reading Kernel Memory from User Space" (USENIX 2018) was the watershed, demonstrating that microarchitectural side effects could shatter the most basic assumption of OS security, that the kernel address space is isolated from user space. Around it, a wave of kernel-fuzzing and exploitation work appeared: "MoonShine: Optimizing OS Fuzzer Seed Selection with Trace Distillation" (USENIX 2018) made syscall fuzzing smarter, while "FUZE: Towards Facilitating Exploit Generation for Kernel Use-After-Free Vulnerabilities" (USENIX 2018) pushed toward automatically judging which kernel bugs are actually exploitable. A parallel thread tackled bloat and isolation at the software level, with "Debloating Software through Piece-Wise Compilation and Loading" (USENIX 2018) and "Security Namespace: Making Linux Security Frameworks Available to Containers" (USENIX 2018), alongside provenance-and-forensics systems like "SAQL" and "Dependence-Preserving Data Compaction for Scalable Forensic Analysis" (both USENIX 2018) aimed at investigating long-running APT campaigns.

By 2019-2020 the field's center of gravity shifted toward fine-grained, in-process isolation, partly as a response to both Spectre/Meltdown-class leaks and the desire for least privilege without full process separation. "ERIM: Secure, Efficient In-process Isolation with Protection Keys (MPK)" (USENIX 2019) showed that Intel MPK could give cheap intra-process compartments, and "Donky" (USENIX 2020) extended that idea to RISC-V and x86. The community then immediately stress-tested the approach: "PKU Pitfalls: Attacks on PKU-based Memory Isolation Systems" (USENIX 2020) exposed real weaknesses in PKU-based schemes, a healthy attack-defense loop. In the browser, "Site Isolation: Process Separation for Web Sites within the Browser" (USENIX 2019) brought the same isolation philosophy to web origins. Meanwhile attack-surface reduction matured from static debloating ("RAZOR", USENIX 2019) into runtime, phase-aware specialization with "Temporal System Call Specialization for Attack Surface Reduction" (USENIX 2020), and kernel access-control analysis advanced through "PeX: A Permission Check Analysis Framework for Linux Kernel" (USENIX 2019) and missing-check detection.

From 2021 onward the work climbed the stack and got more automated. Fuzzing moved beyond the kernel proper to hypervisors and device interfaces, with "Nyx: Greybox Hypervisor Fuzzing using Fast Snapshots and Affine Types" (USENIX 2021) and earlier "USBFuzz" (USENIX 2020), while "SyzVegas: Beating Kernel Fuzzing Odds with Reinforcement Learning" (USENIX 2021) brought learning-based tuning to fuzzers. Isolation expanded to new runtimes and threat models, including "Swivel: Hardening WebAssembly against Spectre" (USENIX 2021) and automatic least-privilege policy generation for microservices (USENIX 2021). The latest listed work, "PROGRAPHER: An Anomaly Detection System based on Provenance Graph Embedding" (USENIX 2023), shows the forensics thread from 2018 coming full circle, now using graph embeddings and learning to detect APTs rather than just record them. Taken together, the area evolved from foundational isolation breaks and basic kernel fuzzing toward a mature ecosystem of cheap hardware-assisted compartments, automated attack-surface reduction, learning-driven testing, and provenance-based detection.

ndss.narrative:
The earliest work in this slice of OS and systems security is dominated by two intertwined problems: reconstructing what attackers did, and stopping them from corrupting memory in the first place. On the forensics side, NDSS 2018 opens with a cluster of provenance and audit-logging papers — "Towards a Timely Causality Analysis for Enterprise Security" (NDSS 2018) and "Towards Scalable Cluster Auditing through Grammatical Inference over Provenance Graphs" (NDSS 2018) — that treat Advanced Persistent Threats as a graph-tracing problem over system logs, while "Fear and Logging in the Internet of Things" (NDSS 2018) extends that same provenance mindset to IoT deployments. In parallel, defenders were hardening the kernel and C++ runtime directly: "K-Miner: Uncovering Memory Corruption in Linux" (NDSS 2018) statically hunts kernel bugs, and "CFIXX: Object Type Integrity for C++" (NDSS 2018) protects the type metadata that control-flow attacks abuse.

Over 2019 and 2020 the two threads matured and scaled. Provenance-based detection moved from tracing to learning normal behavior, with "Unicorn: Runtime Provenance-Based Detector for Advanced Persistent Threats" (NDSS 2020) and the alert-triage system "NoDoze" (NDSS 2019) directly attacking the analyst's alert-fatigue problem, while "OmegaLog" (NDSS 2020) and "Custos" (NDSS 2020) pushed toward higher-fidelity, tamper-evident logs across application and OS layers. At the same time the field broadened its notion of "the OS you can't trust": trusted execution work like "SANCTUARY: ARMing TrustZone with User-space Enclaves" (NDSS 2019) and "Ginseng: Keeping Secrets in Registers When You Distrust the Operating System" (NDSS 2019) built isolation that survives a compromised kernel, and the hardware boundary itself became a target with "Thunderclap" (NDSS 2019) exposing IOMMU/DMA weaknesses. Bug-finding also went systematic, with kernel and hypervisor fuzzing in "HFL: Hybrid Fuzzing on the Linux Kernel" (NDSS 2020) and "HYPER-CUBE: High-Dimensional Hypervisor Fuzzing" (NDSS 2020). This is also when microarchitecture entered the OS-security conversation head-on: "ConTExT: A Generic Approach for Mitigating Spectre" (NDSS 2020).

By 2021 and 2022 the emphasis shifted toward richer log semantics and finer-grained in-kernel isolation. "WATSON" (NDSS 2021) and "ALchemist" (NDSS 2021) tried to abstract attacker behavior and fuse application logs without heavy instrumentation, while "Preventing Kernel Hacks with HAKCs" (NDSS 2022) compartmentalized the kernel and "Kasper" (NDSS 2022) scanned for the generalized transient-execution gadgets that Spectre-era work had warned about. Embedded and real-time systems ran as a steady parallel track throughout — from memory-view switching and return-address integrity in "µRAI" (NDSS 2020) to hotpatching in "HERA" (NDSS 2021) and porting TEEs down to constrained devices in "MyTEE" (NDSS 2023).

The most recent work, clustered in NDSS 2026, shows the field confronting a much wider and messier attack surface than the single Linux host of 2018. Isolation is now studied across CPUs, browsers, and clouds: "Pitfalls for Security Isolation in Multi-CPU Systems" (NDSS 2026) and "Are your Sites Truly Isolated? Automatically Detecting Logic Bugs in Site Isolation Implementations" (NDSS 2026) probe isolation boundaries, while "Breaking the Bulkhead: Demystifying Cross-Namespace Reference Vulnerabilities in Kubernetes Operators" (NDSS 2026) and "Mapping the Cloud" (NDSS 2026) push the same isolation and misconfiguration concerns into orchestrated cloud infrastructure. Kernel exploitation and hardening have also co-evolved into an explicit arms race: "SoK: Take a Deep Step into Linux Kernel Hardening Effectiveness" (NDSS 2026) audits how well defenses actually hold, "DirtyFree: Simplified Data-Oriented Programming in the Linux Kernel" (NDSS 2026) shows attackers routing around Kernel CFI via data-oriented programming, and "PhantomMap: GPU-Assisted Kernel Exploitation" (NDSS 2026) recruits the GPU as a new exploitation primitive. Fuzzing and RTOS isolation, the recurring themes of the middle years, resurface in "HyperMirage" (NDSS 2026) and "IsolatOS" (NDSS 2026), confirming that finding memory-safety and isolation bugs remains an unsolved, continuously escalating problem.

sp.narrative:
The earliest papers here split cleanly along two questions that still define OS and systems security: how do you protect data on a machine you do not fully trust, and how do you find the low-level bugs that let attackers in? On the trust side, EnclaveDB: A Secure Database Using SGX (S&P 2018) showed that a hardware enclave could hold an entire database engine while guaranteeing confidentiality and freshness, an early bet that trusted execution environments would become a foundation rather than a curiosity. On the bug-finding side, Razzer: Finding Kernel Race Bugs through Fuzzing (S&P 2019) pushed fuzzing beyond simple crashes into concurrency, a hard problem that Fuzzing File Systems via Two-Dimensional Input Space Exploration (S&P 2019) and later Krace: Data Race Fuzzing for Kernel File Systems (S&P 2020) and NtFuzz (S&P 2021) carried into file systems and Windows.

A third theme arrived almost immediately and grew fastest: reasoning about attacks from the system's own audit logs. HOLMES: Real-Time APT Detection through Correlation of Suspicious Information Flows (S&P 2019) showed you could correlate suspicious information flows into real-time detection of advanced threats, and Tactical Provenance Analysis for Endpoint Detection and Response Systems (S&P 2020) tied that idea to the EDR products defenders actually run. The mid-period work then made two moves. Provenance analysis turned to machine learning, first as recommendation with SHADEWATCHER (S&P 2022) and graph summarization with DEPCOMM (S&P 2022), while the community took stock of the whole subfield in SoK: History is a Vast Early Warning System (S&P 2023). At the same time, TEEs flipped from something to build to something to break, with SoK: Understanding the Prevailing Security Vulnerabilities in TrustZone-assisted TEE Systems (S&P 2020) cataloguing where deployed enclaves fail.

By 2024 both threads reached maturity. Provenance detection became graph-representation learning in Kairos: Practical Intrusion Detection and Investigation using Whole-system Provenance and Flash (both S&P 2024), with R-CAID (S&P 2024) folding root-cause analysis directly into detection. Meanwhile confidential computing faced sharp offensive results: WeSee: Using Malicious #VC Interrupts to Break AMD SEV-SNP (S&P 2024) broke a modern confidential-VM design through its interrupt interface, echoing the earlier warning that TEE guarantees are only as strong as their weakest interface.

The most recent papers show the field circling back to classic kernel and memory-safety problems with fresh urgency. Memory-corruption defense dominates the 2026 slate: Crashing Through Defenses: Exploiting Segfaults and Chaining Around Intel CET and PLaTypus: Restricting Cross-Module Transitions to Mitigate Code-Reuse Attacks (both S&P 2026) continue the long code-reuse arms race, while QuickSafe: Targeted Hardening Against Memory Corruption (S&P 2026) tackles the adoption gap that keeps memory-safety tools on the shelf. New attack surfaces keep opening too, from remote kernel exploitation in NetPanic: the Attack Surface You Can't Syscall to cache side-channel heap exploitation in HEAP LOCALIZATION (both S&P 2026), even as SoK: All You Ever Wanted to Know About Bootloader Security (S&P 2026) and confidential-cloud rollback work like It's a Feature, Not a Bug (S&P 2026) push the trusted-computing agenda downward into boot and upward into the cloud. The throughline across nearly a decade is consistent: attackers move between layers faster than any single defense can close, and systems security advances by watching the system itself, whether through provenance, formal verification, or ever-harder hardware isolation.

ccs.narrative:
Systems security at CCS has tracked the evolving boundary between kernel isolation, provenance tracking, and attack detection. The 2018 cohort established provenance as a core defensive primitive: Runtime Analysis of Whole-System Provenance (CCS 2018) demonstrated OS-level audit graphs for root-cause analysis, NodeMerge: Template Based Efficient Data Reduction For Big-Data Causality Analysis (CCS 2018) made those graphs tractable at scale, and POIROT: Aligning Attack Behavior with Kernel Audit Records for Cyber Threat Hunting (CCS 2019) operationalized threat-intelligence graphs against live audit logs. Control-flow integrity saw important advances with Enforcing Unique Code Target Property for Control-Flow Integrity (CCS 2018) and Where Does It Go?: Refining Indirect-Call Targets with Multi-Layer Type Analysis (CCS 2019).

Debloating emerged as a complementary attack-surface-reduction strategy, with Effective Program Debloating via Reinforcement Learning (CCS 2018) applying RL to remove unused code from production binaries. Anomaly detection moved toward continuous adaptation with Lifelong Anomaly Detection Through Unlearning (CCS 2019), which prevented false-positive accumulation by unlearning benign patterns.

From 2022, the community grappled with new kernel exploitation primitives such as DirtyCred: Escalating Privilege in Linux Kernel (CCS 2022), which bypassed modern mitigations by swapping credential objects. Provenance-based endpoint detection matured into industrial deployments, as assessed in Are we there yet? An Industrial Viewpoint on Provenance-based Endpoint Detection and Response Tools (CCS 2023).

top4.narrative:
The earliest work in this list splits along two enduring lines. On one side sits the raw mechanics of OS-level isolation and its failures: "Meltdown: Reading Kernel Memory from User Space" (USENIX 2018) showed that the hardware boundary between user and kernel memory could be bypassed through microarchitectural side effects, undercutting the field's most basic assumption, while "MoonShine" (USENIX 2018) sharpened the tooling for finding kernel bugs by distilling syscall traces into good fuzzer seeds. Alongside these, a wave of hardening and attack-surface reduction appeared — "Debloating Software through Piece-Wise Compilation and Loading" (USENIX 2018), "Effective Program Debloating via Reinforcement Learning" (CCS 2018), and control-flow defenses like "Enforcing Unique Code Target Property for Control-Flow Integrity" (CCS 2018). On the other side, "Fear and Logging in the Internet of Things" (NDSS 2018) and "Towards a Timely Causality Analysis for Enterprise Security" (NDSS 2018) began treating system audit logs as a security signal, framing intrusion investigation as a data-provenance problem.

That provenance thread became the area's defining breakthrough over the next few years. "HOLMES" (S&P 2019) correlated suspicious information flows into real-time APT detection, and "NoDoze" (NDSS 2019) and "POIROT" (CCS 2019) attacked alert fatigue and threat hunting over kernel audit records. The approach then shifted from hand-built rules toward learning: "Unicorn" (NDSS 2020) modeled whole-system provenance graphs at runtime, "OmegaLog" (NDSS 2020) fused kernel and application-layer logs, and "WATSON" (NDSS 2021), "SHADEWATCHER" (S&P 2022), and "PROGRAPHER" (USENIX 2023) brought semantic abstraction, recommendation models, and graph embeddings to bear — culminating in "Kairos" (S&P 2024), which unified detection and investigation over whole-system provenance.

In parallel, the isolation-and-hardening line kept advancing. "ERIM" (USENIX 2019) made in-process isolation cheap using Intel MPK, "SANCTUARY" (NDSS 2019) carved user-space enclaves out of ARM TrustZone, and "Razzer" (S&P 2019) and "HFL" (NDSS 2020) drove deeper into kernel race and hybrid fuzzing. SoK papers took stock of the terrain — the perils of hardware performance counters (S&P 2019) and the vulnerabilities pervading TrustZone-assisted TEEs (S&P 2020) — signaling a maturing but fragile foundation.

The most recent work, concentrated in NDSS 2026, shows the field pressing on both the offensive frontier and the newer isolation boundaries that cloud and heterogeneous hardware introduce. Kernel exploitation is being pushed into fresh regimes with "PhantomMap: GPU-Assisted Kernel Exploitation" and "DirtyFree: Simplified Data-Oriented Programming in the Linux Kernel," while "SoK: Take a Deep Step into Linux Kernel Hardening Effectiveness" steps back to ask how much of a decade of defenses actually holds. At the same time, isolation questions have migrated upward and outward — "Breaking the Bulkhead" probes cross-namespace flaws in Kubernetes operators, "Are your Sites Truly Isolated?" finds logic bugs in browser Site Isolation, "Pitfalls for Security Isolation in Multi-CPU Systems" and "IsolatOS" revisit hardware and RTOS boundaries, and "Janus" and "HyperMirage" tackle RDMA-cloud access control and virtual-CPU fuzzing. The through-line from Meltdown holds: isolation remains the central promise of systems security, and each new layer of abstraction reopens it as an unsolved problem.
